ny_s_books_tier.blurb: Books Tier is a cliff band within Powerlinez, in the southwest corner of Harriman State Park near Ramapo, about an hour from New York City. It sits above the Tower Wall and is split into nine sectors with bookish names, such as The Good Book, Check Book, Fairy Tales and Top Shelf. Top-rope lines are the bulk, with a solid group of trad routes and a few bolted ones, and the grades run from 5.3 to 5.11, with most between 5.8 and 5.10. Powerlinez has hard, high-friction gneiss, and the Books Tier rock has more horizontal layers and holds than the lower tiers. The cliffs there are not tall: the highest roped wall at Powerlinez is about 80 feet and most are under 50.

pa_ohiopyle_state_park.blurb: Ohiopyle State Park lies along the Youghiogheny River in the Laurel Highlands of southwestern Pennsylvania, better known for whitewater but also a real climbing and bouldering stop. Bouldering is about two thirds of the climbing, mostly V1 to V5 with some hard problems up to V12. Falls City Boulders, also called The Pyle, is the biggest field, with gritty, textured rock, and Proving Grounds is known for fine stone and highball lines. Sport routes make up most of the rest, mostly 5.10 to 5.12, on steep crags such as Bruner Run, Maple Wall, School House Crag and River's End, some around 100 feet tall. The sport crags get plenty of sun, which makes them a good winter choice. Top-rope options exist for all abilities.

az_kingman_area.blurb: Kingman is a small town in northern Arizona, between Las Vegas and Flagstaff, and the climbing around it is mostly sport, with a fair amount of trad and a small bouldering side of easy problems. Most routes fall between 5.9 and 5.11, with a few moderates and a handful harder. The area has a variety of rock and is still underdeveloped but growing quickly. The Black Mountains near Golden Valley are the main sport area: walls of 40 to 100 feet in the 5.7 to 5.12 range with sunny mornings and shady afternoons, on rock that is easy on the hands with pockets and edges. Beale Springs Wall is in town. Rock quality in the Hualapai Mountains ranges from very poor to great.

ca_cap_rock_area.blurb: Cap Rock sits in the Sheep Pass area of central Joshua Tree National Park, near the Keys View intersection and a short drive from Hidden Valley. Trad climbing leads, backed by a good boulder circuit with mostly easy problems, some top-rope and a little sport and aid. Routes run from 5.3 to 5.12 with the most around 5.8 to 5.10, so there is plenty for moderate climbers. At Cap Rock itself there are slabs, cracks and faces with very short approaches, and it is one of the most popular places to bring beginners. It can be busy, though there is usually room for everyone. Nearby sub-areas include The Hatrack, Top Hat Rock and Rabbit Warren.

ca_horse_flats.blurb: Horse Flats is a high-altitude bouldering area in the Angeles National Forest in the San Gabriel Mountains above Los Angeles, at around 5,600 feet along the Angeles Crest Highway. It feels secluded despite its closeness to the city. The rock is coarse, gritty granite where friction and footwork matter, and the problems range from technical faces to steep overhangs. Most of the climbing is bouldering, with a large share of problems at V0 to V3, a fair number in the V4 to V7 range and a few hard ones, plus a limited set of top-rope problems on the Top Rope Wall. The Main Area has the most. Winters can be very cold, and the best season runs from late spring through fall, with tall pines shading the summer heat.

co_castle_view_crags_boulders.blurb: Castle View lies in the Wonderland section of the South Platte in Colorado and combines roped crags with a large boulder field. Bouldering is most of it, with plenty of V0 to V3 problems and a decent number up to V7 and beyond. The Forest Boulders are in the trees near Puff's Lair, on two kinds of granite: coarse, abrasive South Platte granite and a finer, firmer type. On the roped side, Puff's Lair is the largest crag, joined by Dental Dome and others, with trad, sport and top-rope lines from about 5.4 to 5.12. The crag rock is a mix of granite, gneiss and pegmatite, well featured with pebbles, edges, flakes and cracks, and generally good though loose blocks can appear after freeze and thaw.
